regions.name: Porta Capena
regions.character: The south-eastern approach along the Via Appia: the narrow valley between the Palatine and the Caelian (Via di S. Gregorio), the Porta Capena with the dripping aqueduct over it, the grove of the Camenae and the shrine of Honos and Virtus, then the wedge between the Via Appia and the Via Latina with the tombs of the Scipios, the arches of Drusus, Verus and Trajan, and beyond the Aurelian Wall the Temple of Mars and the bank of the Almo. Baths of Severus and Commodus, the Mutatorium Caesaris (where emperors changed into triumphal dress) and the Area Apollinis. A road and tomb district more than a residential one, though its insulae count is high.
regions.note: Hulsen: it begins at the east corner of the Palatine and, beyond the Aventine, widens to the Almo beyond the Aurelian Wall. The wedge beyond the wall here is a schematic tongue to the Almo crossing of the Via Appia. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Caelimontium
regions.character: Most of the Caelian: the Temple of Divus Claudius on its western brow, the Macellum Magnum (later S. Stefano Rotondo), the barracks of the Castra Peregrina and the 5th cohort of vigiles, the gladiator schools (Ludus Matutinus and Dacicus) and their spoliarium near the Colosseum, and great aristocratic houses (the Laterani, the domus of Philip, the Victiliana, the Valerii, later the Lateran palace and basilica). Nero's arches crossed it. A prosperous, airy hill of domus and barracks.
regions.note: Northern limit the straight street from the Colosseum to the Porta Asinaria (Via di S. Giovanni in Laterano); southern limit the foot of the Caelian toward Region I and the Aurelian Wall. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Isis et Serapis
regions.character: The Colosseum valley and the Oppian: the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Ludus Magnus, the Moneta, the Baths of Titus and Trajan over the ruins of the Domus Aurea, the Porticus of Livia, the Sette Sale cistern and the sanctuary of Isis and Serapis that gave the region its name. Monumental and public in its lower part, residential on the hill.
regions.note: Bounded by Region II, the Servian Wall, the Clivus Suburanus from the Porta Esquilina westward, and a line turning south to the Meta Sudans. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Templum Pacis
regions.character: From the upper Sacra Via and the Velia (Basilica of Maxentius, Temple of Venus and Roma, the Colossus) north through the Templum Pacis into the crowded Subura and up the Cispius to the Servian agger. The Subura was the classic quarter of dense insulae, shops and taverns; the Argiletum its bookselling street; the Tigillum Sororium and the Carinae's grand houses lay on its edges.
regions.note: Hulsen: includes the Sacra Via up to the Atrium Vestae, the Subura and the Cispius; bounded by Region III, the Servian Wall, and the Vicus Patricius from the Porta Viminalis; curves between the fora of Nerva and Vespasian. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Esquiliae
regions.character: The Esquiline plateau outside the Servian agger: once the paupers' necropolis and the grove of Libitina, transformed from the 30s BC into the great horti (Maecenas, Lamia, Taurus, Pallas, Epaphroditus, Licinius, Spes Vetus), with the Nymphaeum of Alexander, the so-called Temple of Minerva Medica, the Macellum Liviae, and the aqueducts converging on Spes Vetus by the Porta Maggiore.
regions.note: In Augustan times it excluded the Campus Viminalis and the land between the Viae Tiburtina and Salaria; by the 4th century its outer edge followed the Aurelian Wall from south of the Via Labicana to the Castra Praetoria, which is how it is drawn here. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Alta Semita
regions.character: The Quirinal and Viminal, named after the 'high path' along the Quirinal ridge (Via XX Settembre): the old temples of Quirinus, Salus and Semo Sancus, the Flavian Temple of the Gens Flavia, the Baths of Constantine and the vast Baths of Diocletian, the Horti Sallustiani in the valley toward the Pincian, the Castra Praetoria and many senatorial houses. Residential and grand.
regions.note: 4th-century limits: the Aurelian Wall around the Castra Praetoria, the Vicus Patricius toward Region IV, and a line down the west foot of the Quirinal to Trajan's Forum. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Via Lata
regions.character: East of the Via Lata (Corso) from the Capitoline foot to the Porta Flaminia, including the Pincian (Collis Hortulorum) with the gardens of Lucullus and the Acilii: the Campus Agrippae and Porticus Vipsania with Agrippa's map, the Arch of Claudius over the road, the Temple of the Sun of Aurelian and the Castra Urbana. A mixed district of porticoes, warehouses and insulae.
regions.note: Lay between the Via Flaminia/Lata and the western limit of Region VI. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Forum Romanum (Forum Magnum)
regions.latin: Regio VIII Forum Romanum vel Magnum
regions.character: The civic heart: the Forum Romanum, the Capitol with the temples of Jupiter and Juno Moneta, the Imperial Fora of Caesar, Augustus and Trajan, the Basilicas Aemilia and Julia, the Velabrum and Vicus Tuscus. The most monumental region, yet it counted 34 vici and 3480 insulae on its fringes.
regions.note: Irregular: the Forum, the imperial fora and the Capitol; on the south a line north of the Forum Boarium through the Velabrum to the east end of the Atrium Vestae. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Circus Flaminius
regions.character: The whole Campus Martius west of the Via Lata to the Tiber: the Circus Flaminius and the temples of the Forum Holitorium and Largo Argentina, the Theatres of Pompey, Balbus and Marcellus with their porticoes, Agrippa's Pantheon and baths, the Saepta, the Stadium and Odeum of Domitian, the Baths of Nero, the Mausoleum of Augustus, the Ara Pacis and Horologium, and the Antonine columns. Largest perimeter of the inner regions and the city's great showcase.
regions.note: All the land between the Servian Wall, the Via Flaminia and the Tiber. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Palatium
regions.character: The Palatine: the hut of Romulus and the archaic sanctuaries, Republican aristocratic houses, the House of Augustus and Temple of Apollo, and from Domitian the imperial palace (Domus Flavia and Augustana) with the Severan extension over the Circus, the Adonaea gardens and the Temple of Elagabalus. The palace dominated, but service quarters and insulae on the slopes give it 2642/2742 insulae.
regions.note: Within the lines of the first pomerium described by Tacitus (Ann. 12.24). Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Circus Maximus
regions.character: The valley of the Circus Maximus with the Forum Boarium and the river port: the round Temple of Hercules Victor, the Temple of Portunus, the Ara Maxima, the Statio Annonae, the Arch of the Argentarii and the Janus Quadrifrons, and the quays by the Pons Aemilius. Commercial and religious, with only 15 balnea and 20 lacus.
regions.note: Very irregular; bounded by the Tiber and Regions IX, VIII, X, XII and XIII. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Piscina Publica
regions.character: The eastern Aventine (Aventinus minor, S. Saba) and the valley of the Via Appia, named after the old public swimming pool: the Baths of Caracalla, the Septem Domus Parthorum, the Cohors IV vigilum, the house of Cilo, and later the Fourth-century mansions. Aristocratic houses among horrea.
regions.note: Bounded by the Via Appia and Region I, the Aurelian Wall, and the vici of the Porta Raudusculana and the Piscina Publica (Viale Aventino line). Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Aventinus
regions.character: The Aventine and the river plain below it: the Temples of Diana, Juno Regina, Minerva and Ceres, the private baths of Sura and Decius, the Armilustrium, then the Emporium, the Porticus Aemilia, the Horrea Galbana and Lolliana and Monte Testaccio, the city's great warehouse and import district. Hence 35 horrea.
regions.note: Between Regions XII and XI, the Aurelian Wall and the Tiber. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

regions.name: Transtiberim
regions.character: Everything on the right bank, with the Tiber Island: the river port and Jewish and Syrian communities of Trastevere, the Naumachia of Augustus and its grove, the Gaianum and the Horti of Caesar, Agrippina and Domitia, the Janiculum with its mills and the Lucus Furrinae, and to the north the Vatican with the Circus of Gaius and Nero, the Phrygianum, Hadrian's Mausoleum and, from Constantine, St Peter's. The largest region by perimeter and the most populous in vici (78).
regions.note: Limits not precisely fixable: it extended beyond the Aurelian Wall south to the Temple of Fors Fortuna and north to take in the Vatican district. Drawn to the Janiculum ridge and the Vatican plain as far as the Mausoleum of Hadrian. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.

servianRegions.name: Suburana
servianRegions.summary: The first of the four Servian regions (Varro LL 5.46-48): the Caelian within the Servian Wall, the Ceroliensis (the low ground of the later Colosseum valley and Carinae edge) and the Subura valley between the Esquiline and the Viminal-Quirinal.
scholarship: Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
servianRegions.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

servianRegions.name: Esquilina
servianRegions.summary: Second Servian region (Varro LL 5.49-50): the Oppius and Cispius with the Fagutal, inside the agger.
scholarship: Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
servianRegions.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

servianRegions.name: Collina
servianRegions.summary: Third Servian region (Varro LL 5.51-52): the Quirinal and Viminal hills (colles) inside the Servian Wall.
scholarship: Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
servianRegions.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

servianRegions.name: Palatina
servianRegions.summary: Fourth Servian region (Varro LL 5.53-54): the Palatium, Germalus and Velia.
scholarship: Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
servianRegions.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

citySummary.source: Breviarium appended to the Curiosum and Notitia (4th century; Notitia readings where they differ in brackets)
citySummary.note: The breviarium gives 46,602 insulae and 1,790 domus, but the regional figures add up to only 44,300 insulae (Notitia readings; 44,400 with the Curiosum's 2,742 for Region X) and about 1,680-1,780 domus; some modern summaries quote 1,797 domus. The 'insulae' probably count rentable units or properties rather than whole blocks (Hermansen; Storey), which is why the totals look implausibly high for buildings. Vicomagistri are 48 per region everywhere (4 per vicus would require 12 vici per region), and the 672 total is 14 x 48. Each region had 2 curatores.
